children: By Konrad Putzier
Inflation picked up in September, a sign that high energy prices are tightening their squeeze on consumers ahead of next month's midterm elections.
The numbers
Consumer prices were up 3.7% in September from a year earlier, the Labor Department said Wednesday, hotter than August's gain of 3.4%.
That was above the 3.6% rise expected by economists surveyed by The Wall Street Journal.
There were signs that high energy prices are starting to leak into other parts of the economy.

Prices excluding food and energy — the so-called core prices, which economists watch to gauge underlying trends — rose 2.6%, above forecasts for a 2.5% increase. Month over month, core prices rose by 0.3%, surprising economists who had expected a 0.2% increase.
"At this point we're at dangerously elevated levels of inflation," said Lindsey Piegza, chief economist at Stifel.
What this means for the midterms

High prices have been a political flashpoint for Americans, who have grown fed up with more than five years of inflation. Prices rose much faster in September than average hourly earnings, which increased 3% from a year earlier, marking the sixth month in a row of inflation outpacing wages. That means many Americans are seeing their real incomes fall.

That dynamic could be costly to Republicans as Americans cast their ballots. Trump's critics say his policies have contributed to inflation: war with Iran on energy, tariffs on goods, and the AI buildout, of which Trump has been an enthusiastic backer, on computer equipment.

President Trump's advisers say that rising prices reflect years of cumulative growth and that the White House's deregulation push will lower prices. The U.S. economy, by many measures, remains resilient.
How the markets reacted
Stocks were down in midday trading. The yield on the 10-year Treasury rose.
Gas and groceries
Energy costs drove inflation in September, and high retail prices in October suggest pain at the pump will continue. Prices have soared since the Iran conflict started at the end of February.
Gasoline prices last month rose 9.1% from the prior month — a faster pace than August's 3.9% increase — and are up 34% over the past year. Fuel-oil prices, meanwhile, are up 74% since last September.

Food prices were flat from the prior month after rising 0.1% in August but are up 2.5% over the past year. Economists are paying attention to food for signs that higher transportation costs are seeping through to prices of goods like meat and dairy.
Where prices really rose
Airfare, which is highly sensitive to fuel costs, was up 22% from a year earlier.

Used car and truck prices rose by 0.7% month over month, up from 0.4% in August, but were down from last year. Prices of goods like apparel and toys, which are often made from petrochemicals, also ticked up.

While oil was the main driver of inflation, price growth also picked up in categories that are less energy sensitive. "This points to broad-based inflation pressure," said Samuel Tombs, chief U.S. economist at Pantheon Macroeconomics.
The cost of recreation services like streaming rose, reflecting "buoyancy in consumer demand," Tombs said. Prices of hospital services also ticked up.
Spiral fears

Some economists see the September report as a worrying sign that the Iran war wasn't just a one-off price shock and that higher inflation is here to stay unless the Federal Reserve acts. "It's already becoming a prolonged issue" seven months into the war, said Stifel's Piegza. One particular concern: Surveys show that consumers now expect higher inflation in the years to come, which can become a self-fulfilling prophecy if they rush into purchases to get ahead of price increases.

Respondents in the University of Michigan's latest consumer survey said they expect inflation of 4.7% over the next year, up from 4.6% in last month's survey. Five-year inflation expectations also rose, to 3.5% from 3.4%.
Other economists are more sanguine, pointing to falling real wages as a sign that inflation is likely to come down again. "Right now the labor market looks weak," said Pantheon's Tombs.
What this means for the Fed

The report raises two questions for Fed officials. The more immediate one is whether they can afford to wait until December to raise rates again after signaling recently that they didn't anticipate moving at their meeting in late October.

Some analysts have argued that there is little reason for the Fed to wait if officials expect to raise rates anyway, though officials haven't given any sign that one report would lead them to reconsider.

Wall Street traders dialed up their bets that the Fed may indeed raise rates when officials meet in two weeks. Traders now see a roughly 40% chance of an October rate hike, up from 22% before the report was released.
The bigger question is how high rates ultimately need to go. That depends on whether pressures from higher energy prices and the AI investment boom are spreading into the broader economy.
Consumer spending

A key reason inflation is stuck above the Fed's target is the strength of America's consumers. Buoyed by low unemployment and rising stock prices, households continue to spend despite rising prices. Executives at the country's biggest banks said this week that higher rates so far haven't dented consumer or business appetite to borrow and spend.
That has all made it easier for businesses to pass on cost increases to their customers.
Data centers
The boom in data-center construction has also contributed to inflation by pushing up the prices of semiconductors and other goods.
Prices for computers, peripherals and smart-home assistants rose 9.7% in September from a year earlier, their biggest annual climb in data going back to 2006.

The challenge for the Fed is that higher interest rates may do little to ease that source of price pressure: Hyperscalers are likely to continue building even if their debt costs rise because the prospect of vast future AI profits is so enticing.
